title: Invertible interval extension in quasicategories
statement: Use simplicial sets, nerves, quasicategories, equivalence edges, universes and $\operatorname{Fun}$ of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], and trivial Kan fibrations of [def-weil-pbc-trivial-kan-fibration]. Let $J=N(\mathcal J)$, where $\mathcal J$ is the ordinary groupoid with objects $0,1$ and exactly one morphism between each ordered pair; let $e_\varepsilon:\Delta^0\to J$ select $\varepsilon$. For a simplicial set $D$, let $hD$ be the category generated by its vertices and edges, with degenerate edges as identities and each $2$-simplex imposing its composition relation. For every quasicategory $D$, two vertices $d_0,d_1$ are isomorphic as objects of $hD$ if and only if there is a simplicial map $J\to D$ taking $0,1$ to $d_0,d_1$ respectively. For every quasicategory $C$ and $\varepsilon=0,1$, endpoint evaluation $e_\varepsilon^*:\operatorname{Fun}(J,C)\to C$ is a trivial Kan fibration. These assertions hold in each input universe, including for empty quasicategories.

source.place: Cisinski, Higher Categories and Homotopical Algebra, July 30, 2026, Theorem 1.6.6 (homotopy-category description), Corollary 3.5.3 (core), Theorem 3.5.11 and Corollaries 3.5.12-3.5.13, printed pp. 106-112. For the endpoint assertion apply 3.5.13 to C -> point and the ordinary Kan-anodyne inclusion {epsilon} -> N(J); h(N(J),C)=Fun(N(J),C), since all edges of this groupoid nerve have inverse triangles. The core argument likewise identifies J-paths with isomorphisms in hD. Here J is the nerve of the walking isomorphism, not Cisinski 3.3.3's freely inverted interval. Compare HTT Proposition 1.2.3.9 and Proposition 1.2.5.3. The combinatorial proofs use outer-horn filling with an invertible edge (3.4.18-3.4.22), not the model-fibrancy theorem 3.6.1 or a comparison with rigidification. Read online 2026-10-17; not archived. No Stacks tag states this interval-extension result.

proof.text: Every simplex of $J$ is a word of vertices $(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$ with $a_i\in\{0,1\}$; a face deletes an entry and a degeneracy repeats one. The edges $u:0\to1$ and $v:1\to0$ have triangles $(0,1,0)$ and $(1,0,1)$ with degenerate long edges. A simplicial map $J\to S$ therefore takes each edge of $J$ to an equivalence edge whenever $S$ is a quasicategory, directly by the inverse-triangle definition in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. In particular, for a map to $D$ with the specified endpoints, the defining triangle relations in $hD$ give $[v][u]=1_{d_0}$ and $[u][v]=1_{d_1}$. Thus such a map implies the required isomorphism of vertices.

source.place: Agent-written nerve-word calculation; compare Section 1.6 and Corollary 1.6.8.

proof.text: Conversely, let $\alpha:d_0\to d_1$ be an isomorphism in $hD$. The edge-representative clause of [lem-coef-homotopy-category-triangle-calculus] gives edges $f:d_0\to d_1$ and $g:d_1\to d_0$ representing $\alpha$ and $\alpha^{-1}$. Its composition-equation clause applied to $[g][f]=[s_0d_0]$ and $[f][g]=[s_0d_1]$ gives actual triangles with spines $(f,g)$ and $(g,f)$ and degenerate long edges. Hence $f$ is an equivalence edge in the precise inverse-triangle sense of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones].

source.place: Theorem 1.6.6 and Corollary 1.6.8, printed pp. 24-25; passage from an ordinary inverse to inverse triangles.

proof.text: Here is the explicit horn filtration used twice below. A nondegenerate simplex of $J$ is exactly an alternating word. Fix $\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}$ and let $w_n=(\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon,\varepsilon,\ldots)$ be the alternating $n$-simplex starting at $\varepsilon$. Start with $J_0=\{\varepsilon\}$ and, for $n\geq1$, adjoin $w_n$ and its missing face $d_0w_n$; denote the generated simplicial subset by $J_n$. All faces $d_iw_n$ for $i>0$ are already in $J_{n-1}$: the last is $w_{n-1}$, and the interior faces have adjacent equal entries and are degeneracies of shorter alternating words. Every proper face of $d_0w_n$ is also already there, by the same deletion calculation. The only new nondegenerate simplices are $w_n$ and $d_0w_n$, so $J_{n-1}\to J_n$ is exactly the attachment along $\Lambda_0^n\hookrightarrow\Delta^n$. For $n=1$ this attaches the other vertex and the forward edge. Both alternating words in every dimension eventually occur, so $\bigcup_nJ_n=J$. With $\varepsilon=0$, $J_1$ is the forward $\Delta^1\subseteq J$, and starting the same filtration at $n=2$ gives $\Delta^1\hookrightarrow J$. Therefore a Kan fibration lifts both endpoint inclusions and $\Delta^1\hookrightarrow J$: choose its horn lift at each stage and take the compatible degreewise union. This is a direct application of horn lifting, including the one-dimensional horn, rather than an appeal to a model structure.

source.place: Agent-written alternating-word filtration of the walking-isomorphism nerve; the horn condition is the Kan condition used in Section 3.5.

proof.text: The terminal map $D\to\Delta^0$ is an isofibration: inner horns fill by the quasicategory hypothesis, and the only equivalence of the point lifts at any vertex to its degenerate identity edge. The core theorem [lem-coef-infinity-core-kan-fibration] makes $D^\simeq\to\Delta^0$ a Kan fibration, so $D^\simeq$ is Kan. The edge $f$ from step 2 factors through $D^\simeq$, since it is an equivalence. Apply the $\Delta^1\hookrightarrow J$ filtration of step 3 to extend $f$ to $J\to D^\simeq\hookrightarrow D$. The endpoints stay $d_0,d_1$. This proves the reverse implication without any use of Joyal-model fibrancy.

source.place: Corollary 3.5.3, printed p. 107, with the explicit interval horn filtration of step 3.

proof.text: Fix $m\geq0$ and a lifting problem for endpoint evaluation with boundary data $a:\partial\Delta^m\to\operatorname{Fun}(J,C)$ and $b:\Delta^m\to C$ satisfying $e_\varepsilon^*a=b|_{\partial\Delta^m}$. Set $K=\partial\Delta^m$, $L=\Delta^m$. Transposing $a$ gives $\widetilde a:J\to\operatorname{Fun}(K,C)$, whose value at $\varepsilon$ is $b|_K$. The terminal map $C\to\Delta^0$ is an isofibration: inner horns fill by the quasicategory condition, and the unique equivalence of $\Delta^0$ lifts at each vertex to the degenerate identity edge. Since $K\hookrightarrow L$ is degreewise injective, [lem-coef-infinity-isofibration-exponentiation] applied to this terminal map makes the restriction $r:\operatorname{Fun}(L,C)\to\operatorname{Fun}(K,C)$ an isofibration between quasicategories. The core theorem [lem-coef-infinity-core-kan-fibration] makes $q=r^\simeq$ a Kan fibration. Step 1, applied to $\widetilde a$, shows that every edge of $J$ is carried to an equivalence in $\operatorname{Fun}(K,C)$; hence every simplex of $\widetilde a$ belongs to its core. The simplex $b$ is a vertex of $\operatorname{Fun}(L,C)$, and every vertex belongs to its core. Thus these data form the genuine lifting square $\{\varepsilon\}\to\operatorname{Fun}(L,C)^\simeq$ over $J\to\operatorname{Fun}(K,C)^\simeq$.

source.place: Theorem 3.5.11 and Corollaries 3.5.12-3.5.13, printed pp. 110-112; restriction to cores and transposition of the lifting problem.

proof.text: Lift the square of step 5 along $q$ using the endpoint filtration of step 3. This produces $\widetilde c:J\to\operatorname{Fun}(L,C)^\simeq$ restricting to $b$ at $\varepsilon$ and mapping under $q$ to $\widetilde a$. Forget its core inclusion and transpose to $c:L\to\operatorname{Fun}(J,C)$. The two triangle equalities of the lifting square say exactly $c|_K=a$ and $e_\varepsilon^*c=b$. For $m=0$, $K=\varnothing$, its functor category is the one-point simplicial set, and the same construction gives a preimage of every vertex $b$; there is no dimension-zero nonemptiness assumption. For $m\geq1$ it gives all boundary fillers. This is precisely the definition of a trivial Kan fibration in [def-weil-pbc-trivial-kan-fibration], so both endpoint evaluations have the required property.

source.place: Direct transposed lifting proof of the specialization of Corollary 3.5.13 to the walking-isomorphism nerve; dimension zero included.

proof.text: All constructions take place in the input universe. The word nerve has finite degree sets, the filtration is countable, and its extensions and degreewise unions involve only simplicial sets of that universe. The core and restriction theorems apply there to the small $K,L$ just used. If $D$ is empty there are no pairs of vertices to check. If $C$ is empty, $\operatorname{Fun}(J,C)$ is empty because $J\times\Delta^m$ has vertices for every $m$; evaluation is the identity of the empty simplicial set, which satisfies all boundary lifting conditions vacuously. Thus neither assertion drops the empty case.

source.place: Agent-written size and empty-input verification of the preceding constructions.

proof_origin.place: Online, not archived: Cisinski Section 1.6 and Section 3.5. The proof specializes the model-independent core/restriction route by an explicit alternating-word horn filtration. No Joyal model-structure, rigidification or interval-extension clause is assumed.

lean.statement: theorem quasicategory_invertible_interval : (∀ (D : SSet.{u}) [Quasicategory D] (d₀ d₁ : D _⦋0⦌), Nonempty ((SSet.hoFunctor.obj.equiv D).symm d₀ ≅ (SSet.hoFunctor.obj.equiv D).symm d₁) ↔ ∃ g : SSet.coherentIso.{u} ⟶ D, g.app _ SSet.coherentIso.x₀ = d₀ ∧ g.app _ SSet.coherentIso.x₁ = d₁) ∧ (∀ (C : SSet.{u}) [Quasicategory C], modelCategoryQuillen.I.rlp (evaluation SSet.coherentIso C SSet.coherentIso.x₀) ∧ modelCategoryQuillen.I.rlp (evaluation SSet.coherentIso C SSet.coherentIso.x₁))
